events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: Status: filed as ethereum/ERCs pull request #2155 ; number ERC-8490 assigned on 2026-11-09. Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?

events.excerpt: For developers building multi-agent systems , the design of information disclosure policies is a critical variable. A preprint published on Nov. 5, 2026 , examines how the precision of information provided to large language models (LLMs) affects their performance in trade and negotiation. The study suggests that increasing information does not consistently improve performance; instead, outcomes are highly dependent on the specific model and the structure of the market. The researchers evaluated ten LLMs across three controlled environments: multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions. To isolate the impact of information, they held models, incentives, and market rules constant while varying the input levels. In trade, least disclosure provides agents with their own values, coarse disclosure adds the counterparty’s ordinal ranking, and full disclosure provides exact values. In bargaining, coarse information only signals whether a mutually profitable price exists, while full disclosure reveals buyer value and seller cost. In double auctions, least disclosure gives own value or cost, coarse adds within-side rankings, and full disclosure provides exact values or costs. Folding the whole leanVM step relation runs at 260 ns per witness element, against leanVM’s 55 ns per committed word (Verified rates). events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . events.excerpt: This is fascinating : The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening. It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another. […] It’s sound that’s relevant here, though, and specifically the sound of aeroplanes. Early in his video, Colsto brings up a map of the flights that were in the air at the time the video he’s tracing was recorded. Much of this information is publicly available. Aircraft equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) transmit data about their position, velocity, and altitude, which flight-tracking services collect and make available to the public. While not every plane is tracked, the system provides an enormous amount of information about aircraft movements.
